description: Org-level process standards: the ticket/branch/PR workflow, the product docs -> capability -> user story + Gherkin -> test case -> implementation -> evidence traceability chain, ADR governance, and code/test hygiene that apply to every project installing AI Agile.

standards.title: No work without a ticket: one issue = one branch = one draft PR (1:1:1)
standards.description: No work begins without a GitHub issue (ticket). Every distinct piece of work — including small fixes — traces 1:1:1 to exactly one issue: one issue → one branch (cut from main) → one draft PR. Never combine multiple issues into one branch or PR, never open more than one PR per issue, and never stack new work onto an existing open PR or reuse a feature branch from a prior session.
standards.rationale: A ticket-first, one-to-one issue/branch/PR mapping makes every change traceable to its rationale and reviewable; unticketed or stacked work entangles unrelated changes and loses traceability.
acceptance_criteria: The change under review traces to exactly one GitHub issue (ticket); no unticketed work.
The branch was cut from main for that single issue, not reused from a prior session's feature branch.
There is exactly one open PR for the issue, and the diff does not bundle changes belonging to a separate issue.
anti_patterns: Starting work or opening a PR with no GitHub issue behind it.
Adding a second issue's fix as extra commits on an existing open PR.
Reusing last session's `claude/...` branch for new, unrelated work.
Two open PRs both claiming to close the same issue.

standards.title: Open a draft PR before the second commit
standards.description: The sequence is: create branch from main → first commit → open a draft PR → continue work. A multi-commit session must not proceed without a live draft PR. Lift out of draft only when CI is green and review is clean.
standards.rationale: An early draft PR makes work visible and CI-checked from the first commit; deferring the PR hides in-progress work from review and CI.
acceptance_criteria: A PR exists in draft state by the time the branch has more than one commit.
The PR was opened as a draft, not as ready-for-review, while work was ongoing.
The PR is taken out of draft only after CI is green.
anti_patterns: Pushing five commits to a branch with no PR open.
Opening a non-draft PR before CI has run.

standards.title: Branches and PRs follow an issue-traceable naming convention
standards.description: Branch and PR names trace to their issue: the branch name includes the issue number and a short slug; the PR title follows a conventional `type(scope): description (#<N>)`; the PR body includes `Closes #<N>` so GitHub auto-links and closes the issue on merge.
standards.rationale: Consistent, issue-traceable naming and the Closes link create a durable git relationship between branch, PR, and issue.
acceptance_criteria: The branch name in the diff includes the issue number and a short slug (this project: `claude/issue-<N>-<slug>`), unless a session assigned a specific branch name.
The PR title follows `type(scope): description (#<N>)`.
The PR body contains `Closes #<N>` referencing the issue.
anti_patterns: A branch name with no issue number.
A PR body with no `Closes #N`, leaving the issue unlinked.

standards.title: Confirm before destructive or shared-infra operations
standards.description: The workflow is permissive and implement-directly, except that operations which are destructive (deleting files, dropping database objects, force-pushing) or affect shared infrastructure (database migrations, CI/CD workflows) require explicit confirmation before proceeding, as does any case where context is insufficient to proceed safely.
standards.rationale: Permissive flow keeps velocity high while still gating the irreversible and the shared-blast-radius operations. Source: .github/copilot-instructions.md §Project-Specific Exceptions (Exception 3).
acceptance_criteria: Destructive operations (file deletion, dropping DB objects, force-push) in the diff were explicitly confirmed before execution.
Changes to database migrations or GitHub Actions workflows in the diff were confirmed before being made.
Where context was insufficient to proceed safely, the work paused for clarification rather than guessing.
anti_patterns: Force-pushing or dropping a table without explicit confirmation.
Editing a CI workflow as an incidental side effect with no confirmation.

standards.title: Express intent in specs, coverage via the BDD .feature, gaps in the roadmap — one place each
standards.description: Every behaviour has three expressions, each in exactly one place: a Product/Capability Specification states what must be true (future/invariant voice); the Gherkin .feature (generated from the user story) and its test evidence state what is proven now; the roadmap and issues own the gap between intent and coverage. No hand-maintained coverage table exists (DOC-004), and no single artefact mixes intent, coverage, and gap.
standards.rationale: Separating intent, coverage, and gap keeps each artefact trustworthy and lets a reader answer 'what does it do?' vs 'what's proven?' without inference; mixing them, or hand-maintaining coverage, makes all three rot. Source: docs/_process/02_product-led-design.md.
acceptance_criteria: A behaviour change in the diff updates a Product/Capability Specification (future/invariant voice), not a 'we test that…' claim.
A coverage change in the diff is reflected in the BDD .feature's executable test / evidence, not a hand-maintained coverage doc.
A gap (missing/flaky/failing test, known regression) is recorded in the roadmap / a GitHub issue, not a markdown gap table.
anti_patterns: A specification that says 'we test that X' instead of stating the invariant 'X'.
A hand-maintained markdown coverage/gap table duplicating what should be the test evidence or the roadmap/issues.

standards.title: Every PR touches the artefacts its change type requires
standards.description: Before opening a PR, answer three questions: does it change behaviour? → a Product/Capability Specification (and its BDD .feature) changes; does it change what is proven? → the BDD .feature and/or its executable test changes; does it create or close a gap? → the roadmap and/or a GitHub issue changes state. A PR that answers no to all three is a pure refactor and says so. The PR description makes intent (spec changes), coverage (.feature/test changes), and gap (roadmap/issue state) explicit.
standards.rationale: Tying each change type to the artefacts it must touch keeps specs, tests, and backlog in lockstep with code.
acceptance_criteria: A behaviour-changing PR in the diff updates the relevant Product/Capability Specification.
A coverage-changing PR updates the BDD .feature and/or lands the executable test.
The PR description states intent, coverage, and gap, or marks itself a pure refactor.
anti_patterns: A feature PR that adds behaviour with no product-doc change.
A bug-fix PR with no regression test and no `closes #N`.

standards.title: Every issue carries one type, one area, and one feature label
standards.description: Every GitHub issue carries exactly one label from each of three orthogonal dimensions: type (type:enhancement | type:debt | type:bug), area (area:testing|docs|security|data-model|performance|ux|infra), and feature (feature:entity-crud|mcp|workflow-engine|frontend|ai-chat|exports). The issue states the gap it closes and its acceptance, not just a title. The portable rule is exactly one label per dimension; the specific area/feature label values are this project's.
standards.rationale: A consistent three-dimensional taxonomy keeps the backlog searchable and triage-able long after filing.
acceptance_criteria: An issue created in the PR carries exactly one type:, one area:, and one feature: label.
The issue states the gap it closes and its acceptance, not just a title.
type/area/feature are chosen per the taxonomy (enhancement adds, bug fixes, debt cleans up).
anti_patterns: An issue with no type label, or two area labels.
A one-line issue with no acceptance criteria or gap description.

standards.title: The Gherkin spec is the authoritative testable spec, generated from the user story
standards.description: Each user story (realising a capability, STD-PROC-013) generates a BDD specification -- a Gherkin .feature that is the authoritative testable specification of the required behaviour and acceptance criteria. The .feature is realised by executable step definitions which produce evidence; the test code realises the .feature and is not itself the source of truth. The chain is capability -> user story -> Gherkin .feature -> test -> evidence. Applies to both API and web behaviour; pure unit tests are out of scope.
standards.rationale: Generating the testable spec from the user story keeps the acceptance criteria, the tests, and the evidence in lockstep with the stated behaviour, and prevents test code from silently becoming the de-facto spec.
acceptance_criteria: Behaviour introduced in the diff is specified as a Gherkin .feature generated from its user story, not asserted only in ad-hoc test code.
The .feature is the source of truth; step definitions realise it and produce evidence.
The chain capability -> user story -> .feature -> test -> evidence is intact for the behaviour in the diff.
anti_patterns: Asserting new behaviour only in test code with no generating Gherkin .feature, or treating the test code as the specification.

standards.title: Work is product-led and AI-first: humans define intent, AI executes, evidence proves
standards.description: All work flows in one direction along a linear, generative chain: Product Specification -> Capability -> User Story (with Gherkin acceptance criteria) -> Test -> Implementation -> Evidence. Humans define intent and govern -- approving product intent, capabilities, user stories and their BDD, architecture, security, evidence, and releases; AI performs the decomposition, generation, implementation, verification, and reporting. Product specifications are the desired state; code plus verified evidence are the current state; the roadmap (STD-PROC-014) is the calculated gap. Work never starts from code or tests -- it starts from the product specification.
standards.rationale: A single product-led, AI-first direction keeps intent authoritative and execution traceable; starting from code or tests divorces delivery from intent and lets the two drift. Source: docs/_process/01_ai-first-product-engineering.md; 04_ai-agile-implementation.md.
acceptance_criteria: New behaviour in the diff originates from a Product/Capability Specification (intended state) and flows capability → BDD → test → implementation → evidence, not from code/tests authored first.
Human approval control points are honoured for the change (intent, capability, BDD, architecture, security, evidence, release).
The gap between desired state (specs) and current state (code + evidence) is reflected in the calculated roadmap (STD-PROC-014), not declared manually.
anti_patterns: Implementing code with no product/capability specification source.
Treating the code or current tests as the definition of intended behaviour.
Hand-maintaining roadmap/status instead of deriving it from evidence.

standards.title: Record significant decisions as ADRs; waive standards only via an ADR citing the STD ID
standards.description: Significant or cross-cutting decisions — architecture, security posture, data-model, or process choices future work must respect — are recorded as Architecture Decision Records in docs/adr/ (NNNN-title.md with status, context, decision, consequences). A waiver of an adr_overridable standard is itself a decision: it is recorded in standards/adrs.json with authorises_exception_to citing the STD ID. Soft-wording a standard to dodge it, or reversing a recorded decision without a superseding ADR, is not permitted.
standards.rationale: ADRs keep the rationale behind durable decisions discoverable and prevent silent re-litigation; routing standard waivers through ADRs makes every exception explicit and auditable.
acceptance_criteria: A significant/cross-cutting decision in the diff is recorded as an ADR in docs/adr/ (status, context, decision, consequences).
A waiver of an adr_overridable standard in the diff is recorded in standards/adrs.json citing the STD ID in authorises_exception_to, not by softening the standard text.
The diff does not reverse a decision an ADR already records without a superseding ADR (STD-DOC-001).
anti_patterns: Making a cross-cutting architectural choice with no ADR capturing the rationale.
Bypassing an adr_overridable standard by rewording it instead of filing an ADR waiver.

standards.title: Fix small in-scope problems now; raise a ticket only when out of scope or too large
standards.description: When a defect, inconsistency, or small improvement is visible while working the current ticket and is simple and within that ticket's scope/mandate, fix it now — do not defer it. Raise a new GitHub issue only when the work is outside the current ticket's scope/mandate or too large to fix inline. Deferring solvable, in-scope work into a new ticket is not permitted. (Process-scoped instance of org STD-ARCH-006 fix-now and STD-ARCH-007 don't-open-issues-for-current-PR-work, framed by the ticket's scope.)
standards.rationale: Fixing simple in-scope problems immediately keeps the codebase from accumulating debt and avoids backlog clutter from issues that are statistically unlikely to be actioned; raising a ticket is reserved for genuinely out-of-scope or large work.
acceptance_criteria: A simple defect/improvement within the current ticket's scope is fixed in the diff, not deferred to a new issue.
A new issue raised in the diff/PR is justified as outside the current ticket's scope/mandate or too large to fix inline.
No TODO/FIXME or placeholder issue substitutes for an in-scope fix that could be made now.
anti_patterns: Filing a follow-up issue for a one-line fix that is in scope and simple.
Leaving a TODO for a defect that could be fixed within the current ticket.
Splitting an in-scope coherent change into a separate ticket to shrink the current run.

standards.title: Every artefact is directly generated from its upstream source and is backward-traceable
standards.description: Delivery follows one generative chain -- product documentation -> capability -> user story (with Gherkin acceptance criteria) -> test case -> implementation -> evidence -- in which each artefact is generated directly from the one before it, never hand-authored independently of its upstream source. Each artefact carries a stable identifier and explicit links to its adjacent artefacts, forming a product knowledge graph traversable forward (what realises this intent?) and backward (why does this code, test, or failure exist?). No artefact appears without a clear upstream source.
standards.rationale: Direct generation with explicit links makes every line of code and every test traceable to the intent that required it, and every intent traceable to its realisation -- the basis of calculated coverage, gap, and impact analysis.
acceptance_criteria: Each artefact introduced in the diff is generated from, or explicitly linked to, its immediate upstream artefact in the chain (product docs -> capability -> user story + Gherkin -> test -> implementation -> evidence).
No artefact in the diff appears without a clear upstream source.
Adjacent artefacts carry stable identifiers linking them forward and backward.
anti_patterns: Hand-authoring a test, or writing implementation code, with no upstream user story / Gherkin scenario it is generated from or linked to.

standards.title: The capability is the canonical unit of product, roadmap, and delivery
standards.description: Capabilities are the primary unit of AI-first delivery and the bridge between product design, roadmap planning, and verification. A product is a collection of capabilities, each a discrete business outcome named in business language. Work enters delivery as a capability — with a stable id, product source, business description, linked outcome, BDD status, and dependencies — not as a vague task; a capability missing these is flagged before implementation. Capabilities are defined once (a Capability Specification, STD-DOC-006) and referenced by id from product specs, the roadmap, BDD specs, and evidence, never duplicated.
standards.rationale: Centring delivery on capabilities keeps product intent, planning, and verification on one shared unit humans and AI can reason over; task-centric work loses that thread.
acceptance_criteria: Work entering implementation in the diff is a capability (stable id, source, description, linked outcome, BDD status, dependencies), not a vague task.
Capabilities in the diff are defined once and referenced by id elsewhere, not redefined across roadmap/spec/tests.
PRs/commits in the diff reference the capability id(s) they deliver.
anti_patterns: Implementing a 'task' with no capability behind it.
Duplicating capability details across roadmap, product spec, and tests instead of referencing the capability id.

standards.title: The roadmap is calculated from evidence: Phase → Outcome → Capability
standards.description: The roadmap (docs/product/roadmap.yaml) is a calculated representation of the gap between desired and current-verified state, structured Phase → Outcome → Capability. It references capabilities by id; it does not redefine modules/components or duplicate capability detail. Status is derived, never hand-maintained: capability status (Not Defined / Defined / Specified / In Progress / Verified / Failed / Blocked) rolls up to outcome progress (verified required capabilities / total) and then to phase progress. Human-readable roadmap views may be generated from the YAML but are not the source of truth.
standards.rationale: Deriving roadmap status from capability evidence keeps it truthful and current; manually maintained status drifts.
acceptance_criteria: Roadmap changes in the diff are made in docs/product/roadmap.yaml as Phase → Outcome → Capability, referencing capabilities by id.
Capability/outcome/phase status in the diff is derived from verification evidence, not hand-set.
Any human-readable roadmap doc in the diff is generated, not a hand-maintained source of truth.
anti_patterns: Hand-setting a capability/outcome/phase to 'done' independent of its evidence.
Redefining modules/components or duplicating capability detail inside the roadmap.

standards.title: Measure undelivered-capability gap and technical-debt gap separately
standards.description: The total product gap has two distinct parts: the undelivered-capability gap (capabilities the roadmap requires that are not yet verified) and the technical-debt gap (delivered, verified capabilities that do not meet the required engineering, quality, security, reliability, or maintainability standard). They are tracked separately. A technical-debt item is linked to its capability, the technical standard it violates, and a remediation recommendation; it is identified during implementation/review and explicitly accepted or scheduled, never silently carried.
standards.rationale: A product can be functionally complete yet carry heavy technical debt; conflating the two hides real risk. Separating them lets humans make informed trade-offs.
acceptance_criteria: Undelivered capabilities in the diff are tracked as roadmap gap (STD-PROC-014), not conflated with technical debt.
A technical-debt item in the diff is linked to its capability, the technical standard it violates, and a remediation recommendation, and is explicitly accepted or scheduled.
A verified capability carrying known debt records that debt rather than presenting as fully complete.
anti_patterns: Recording a delivered-but-substandard capability as simply 'done' with the debt unrecorded.
Mixing undelivered-capability gap and technical-debt gap in one untyped metric.

standards.title: GitHub Actions workflow names follow TYPE - Description format
standards.description: Every GitHub Actions workflow `name:` field must follow the pattern `{TYPE} - {Description}` where TYPE is a single uppercase keyword identifying the workflow category (e.g. BUILD, DEPLOY, SYNC, VALIDATE, REGRESSION, LINT, RELEASE, SETUP, CONTROL, PROCESS, ORCHESTRATE) and Description is a complete active sentence with a verb that fully describes what the workflow does. The separator is a space-hyphen-space ( - ). Both the type and description must appear on the top-level `name:` key, not only in the job name. DEPLOY workflows use the target platform as the description rather than a verb sentence: `DEPLOY - {Platform}` (e.g. `DEPLOY - AWS`, `DEPLOY - Azure`). When multiple deploy workflows exist for the same platform, append a service qualifier: `DEPLOY - {Platform} - {Service}` (e.g. `DEPLOY - Azure - Communications Services`, `DEPLOY - Azure - Static Web App`).
standards.rationale: A consistent prefix makes the Actions tab scannable: developers see the category at a glance without reading the full name. An active sentence for the description ensures the name is self-contained and unambiguous when it appears in notifications, status badges, and CI logs.
acceptance_criteria: The workflow `name:` starts with an uppercase TYPE keyword drawn from the approved vocabulary (BUILD, DEPLOY, SYNC, VALIDATE, REGRESSION, LINT, RELEASE, SETUP, CONTROL, PROCESS, ORCHESTRATE, or another uppercase category approved for the project).
The TYPE is followed by exactly ` - ` (space, hyphen, space).
For non-DEPLOY workflows, the description after ` - ` is a complete active sentence containing a verb that fully describes what the workflow does without requiring knowledge of the filename.

For DEPLOY workflows, the description is the target platform name (`DEPLOY - AWS`, `DEPLOY - Azure`). When multiple deploy workflows exist for the same platform, a service qualifier is appended (`DEPLOY - Azure - Communications Services`).
No emoji or non-ASCII characters appear in the `name:` field.
anti_patterns: name: Pipeline Orchestrator  -- no type prefix, not a sentence.
name: Sync .claude directory  -- no type prefix.
name: CI  -- too terse; no information about what CI does.
name: deploy  -- lowercase type, not a sentence.
name: BUILD: compile the app  -- colon separator instead of space-hyphen-space.
name: SYNC - sync files  -- description repeats the type word rather than saying what is synced.
name: DEPLOY - Deploy to Azure  -- verb in description is redundant; use DEPLOY - Azure.
name: DEPLOY - Azure  -- ambiguous when three Azure workflows exist; qualify with the service name.
